Content:
Consider an object shot straight up from the surface of the Earth, assuming the only force acting on the object is gravity (ignore air resistance and any thrust). How do we model its velocity?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/88baaebcbae507581d03ae7badd27c86]

Content:
According to Newton's law of gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward Earth is
[MATH: F_\text{in} = G\dfrac{mM}{r^2},]
where

Content:
- [MATH: G] is the gravitational constant,
- [MATH: m] is the mass of the object,
- [MATH: M] is the mass of the Earth, and
- [MATH: r=r(t)] is the distance between their centers of mass.

Content:
At the initial position, when the object is on the surface of the Earth, [MATH: r] equals the radius of the planet [MATH: R.]

Content:
Then, taking the outward direction as positive and applying Newton's second law, [MATH: F=ma,] where [MATH: a] is the acceleration of the object, we have
[MATH: F|= − F_{in}; ma|= − G(mM)/(r^{2}); a|= − (GM)/(r^{2}).]
In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,
[MATH: a=\dfrac{k}{r^2},]
with constant of proportionality [MATH: k=-GM<0.]

Content:
To find [MATH: k,] we use the conditions at the Earth's surface. When [MATH: r=R] (Earth's radius), the acceleration is [MATH: a=-g] (where [MATH: g] is standard gravity). Substituting these values:
[MATH: -g = \dfrac{k}{R^2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k = -gR^2.]
Substituting [MATH: k] back into our equation for acceleration, we obtain
[MATH: a = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}.]

Content:
Now, since [MATH: a=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}] and [MATH: v=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t},] we can express acceleration as a derivative of velocity with respect to distance [MATH: r] as follows (treating [MATH: v] as a function of [MATH: r] along the trajectory):
[MATH: a|= (dv)/(dt); = (dv)/(dr) ⋅ (dr)/(dt); = (dv)/(dr) ⋅ v; = v(dv)/(dr).]
Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:
[MATH: v\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}r} = -\dfrac{gR^2}{r^2}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider an object shot straight up from the surface of the Earth, assuming the only force acting on the object is gravity (ignore air resistance and any thrust). How do we model its velocity?

[IMG: /graphics/88baaebcbae507581d03ae7badd27c86]

According to Newton's law of gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward Earth is

Content:

- [MATH: m] is the mass of the object,
- [MATH: M] is the mass of the Earth, and
- [MATH: r=r(t)] is the distance between their centers of mass.

[MATH: F|= − F_{in}; ma|= − G(mM)/(r^{2}); a|= − (GM)/(r^{2}).]
